claims.text: CrCoNi and Fe80−xMnxCo10Cr10 can possess metastable FCC structures at ambient and cryogenic conditions.
The proposed initial alloy state is a nearly random solid solution with low short-range order.
Local chemical short-range order and hard atomic motifs generate spatial fluctuations in shear-fault or stacking-fault energy.
Fluctuations in shear-fault energy, rather than its globally averaged value, are a governing origin of strength in complex concentrated alloys.
Local chemical and fault-energy fluctuations govern unusual deformation behavior in metastable concentrated alloys.
Sites with high local shear-fault energy pin dislocations.
Local short-range order and spatial fault-energy fluctuations produce non-planar or wavy dislocation paths.
Enhanced local fault-energy fluctuations promote deformation twinning.
Dislocation interactions with local fault-energy fluctuations increase effective alloy strength.
The proposed mechanism delays conventional dislocation glide and failure.
A thermal or thermomechanical treatment can increase short-range order without causing phase separation or significant grain growth.
Increasing short-range order by treatment will increase both yield strength and ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Increasing short-range order will produce more pronounced wavy dislocation configurations than in the baseline alloy.
Increasing short-range order will produce more deformation twinning than in the baseline alloy.
Twinning can be a primary deformation mode in metastable FCC Fe80−xMnxCo10Cr10, CrMnFeCoNi, and CrCoNi alloys.
The hypothesis should hold from ambient to cryogenic temperatures.
The hypothesis should hold under quasi-static deformation rates.
The mechanism should generalize to chemically complex alloys with similar metastable FCC structures and chemically sensitive intrinsic energy barriers.
The untreated random-solid-solution baseline has a spatially uniform shear-fault energy and conventional dislocation glide.

contradictions.description: The baseline describes a random multicomponent alloy as having spatially uniform shear-fault energy, whereas the central hypothesis treats local chemical and fault-energy fluctuations as characteristic of chemically complex alloys. A globally averaged fault energy is not equivalent to local spatial uniformity, so the baseline conflates these concepts.
